The title and Wŏnhyo’s introductions

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 1 THE AWAKENING OF FAITH⁕

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

My explanation of this treatise has three main parts. First I state its guiding theme and its essence. ↓ Next I explain the title. ↓ Third I follow the text to bring out its meaning. ↓

1. The guiding theme and essence of the treatise

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

First, the guiding theme and essence. The Great Vehicle in its essence is empty and still, fathomless in its quiet depths. † Profound beyond profundity, how could it lie outside the myriad appearances? Still beyond stillness, it remains within the discourse of the hundred schools. Though it lies within appearances, even the five eyes cannot see its body. Though it is present within words, even the four kinds of eloquence cannot describe its form. Call it great, and it enters even what has no inside, leaving nothing out. Call it minute, and it enfolds what has no outside, with room to spare. Draw it toward existence, and the one suchness, in its operation, is empty. Take it for nonexistence, and the myriad things ride on it and come into being. Lacking words for it, we give it the makeshift name “Great Vehicle.” Apart from the great being who kept silent and the adept who understood at a glance, who could discourse on the Great Vehicle where words fall away, or arouse deep faith where thought comes to an end?

Great Vehicle · 大乘 dà shèng · BDK p. 3 Mahayana · Mahāyāna
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Accordingly the bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, with great compassion that takes no object, grieved that the delusive wind of ignorance stirs the ocean of mind and so easily sets beings adrift. † He pitied those whose true nature of original awakening slumbers in a long dream from which they can scarcely wake. † Through the power of wisdom that knows a common essence, he could compose this treatise and expound the recondite meaning of the Tathāgata’s profound sūtras. He wanted students, by opening a single scroll for a moment, to explore the whole purport of the three baskets of scripture. He wanted followers of the path to put the myriad objects to rest once and for all and so return to the source of the one mind.

ignorance · 無明 wú míng · BDK p. 25 nonenlightenment (avidyā) · avidyā · Hakeda usually calls 無明 ‘ignorance’. His parallel here pairs 無明 with 無漏.
original awakening · 本覺 běn jué · BDK p. 17 original enlightenment
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Its exposition is extensive, but one may express it briefly. By opening two gateways within the one mind, it gathers up the vast teaching of the 108 [questions of the Laṅkāvatāra] at Mount Malaya. † By showing purity of nature amid the characteristics of defilement, it draws together the subtle intent of the fifteen [chapters of Queen Śrīmālā’s discourse] at Ayodhyā. Consider the teaching of a single taste at the Crane Grove, the purport of nonduality at Vulture Peak, the three bodies as the ultimate fruit in the Golden Drum and the Sūtra of Sameness, the four stages as profound causes in the Flower Adornment and the Jeweled Necklace, the vast expanse of the highest path in the Large Perfection of Wisdom and the Great Collection, and the subtle, hidden gateways of the Sun Treasury and the Moon Treasury. What other treatise runs a single thread through the heart of all these scriptures? Hence the text says below, “To gather up all the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma, this treatise should be expounded.”

two gateways · 二門 èr mén · BDK p. 11 two aspects
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Such being the treatise’s intent, in its expanded exposition it takes immeasurable and boundless meanings as its guiding theme. In its condensed exposition it takes the Dharma of the two gateways and one mind as its essential point. The two gateways encompass myriad meanings without confusion. The boundless meanings blend together, for they share the one mind. Thus it freely expands or condenses its teaching and can establish or refute a position without impediment. It expands without prolixity and condenses without constriction. In establishing a position it gains nothing, and in refuting one it loses nothing. Such is Aśvaghoṣa’s wondrous art and the guiding theme and essence of the Awakening of Faith.

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

The treatise’s purport runs so deep that few commentators have grasped its guiding theme in full. Each holds fast to what he has learned and pulls the text in that direction, unable to clear his mind and seek its intent. Thus they fall short of the author’s intention. Some look toward the source and lose the stream. Some grasp the leaves and forget the trunk. Some cut away the collar to mend the sleeve. Some break off a branch and take the root with it. I shall follow the wording of the treatise itself and match its passages with the scriptures it expounds. I hope that those who share this aim will weigh the matter for themselves. This concludes the statement of its guiding theme and essence.

2. The title

1. Great Vehicle

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Next comes the explanation of the title. In “Great Vehicle,” “great” names a quality of the Dharma itself. It means that the Dharma embraces all. “Vehicle” names it by analogy. A vehicle serves to carry beings along. So much for the general explanation. The detailed explanation proceeds in two ways, first by way of the sūtras, then by way of the treatises. ↓ ↓

1. The sūtras
The extent of the vehicle
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

For the scriptural account, the Ākāśagarbha Sūtra says, “The Great Vehicle is immeasurable, without boundary or limit, pervading all things like space. So vast is it that it can accommodate all sentient beings. It extends beyond what disciples and solitary buddhas have in common. For these reasons it is called the Great Vehicle.”

The parts and operation of the vehicle
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Again, as for the vehicle, steadfast practice of the four means of gathering beings forms its wheels. The ten skillful courses of action, thoroughly purified, form its spokes. Its store of pure merit forms its hub. Firm, wholehearted resolve forms its axle fittings, linchpins, pegs, and clasps. Mastery of the meditative absorptions and liberations forms its shafts. The four immeasurables keep [its horses] well trained. Admirable friends are its charioteers. Knowing the right and wrong times determines when it sets out. The proclamation of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and not-self is its goad. The jeweled cords of the seven factors of awakening form its harness and traces.⁕ The purified five eyes are its straps and bindings. Great compassion, universal in scope and upright in intent, is its streaming banner. The four right efforts form its brace (the crosspiece supporting the wheel). The four establishments of mindfulness keep it level and straight. The four bases of success give it speed. The five superior powers form its defensive array [the vehicle term is uncertain]. The noble eightfold path is its straight course. The unobstructed light of wisdom concerning all beings forms its carriage. With the six perfections practiced without settling anywhere, it directs merit toward omniscience. With unobstructed [knowledge of] the four truths, it crosses to the further shore. This is the Great Vehicle. My explanation is that these twenty clauses draw an analogy to illustrate the Dharma and bring out the meaning of “vehicle.”

The vehicle in relation to beings
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

The sūtra also says further on, “This vehicle the buddhas receive, disciples and solitary buddhas contemplate, and all bodhisattvas ride. Śakra, Brahmā, and the world guardians should pay it homage. All sentient beings should make offerings to it. All who are wise should praise it. The whole world should turn to it for refuge. No Māra can destroy it. No teacher of another path can fathom it. Nothing in the world can rival it.” My explanation is that these ten clauses illustrate the Great Vehicle through the beings who encounter it.

2. The treatises
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

The treatises explain greatness under seven headings or three. The three meanings of “great” will be explained below. ↓ As for the seven, there are two sets of seven. ↓ ↓

1. Seven kinds of greatness in the Abhidharma treatise
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

First, the Abhidharma treatise says, “It is called the Great Vehicle because it possesses seven kinds of greatness. What are the seven?”

1. Object
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

“First, greatness of object. The bodhisattva path takes as its object the vast teachings of hundreds of thousands of sūtras, too many to measure.

2. Practice
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Second, greatness of practice. One rightly undertakes all the far-reaching practices that benefit oneself and others.

3. Wisdom
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Third, greatness of wisdom. One understands the full scope of the selflessness of persons and dharmas.

4. Persistence
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Fourth, greatness of persistence. Over three incalculable periods of great eons, one diligently and skillfully cultivates immeasurably many difficult practices.

5. Skill in means
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Fifth, greatness of skill in means. † One abides neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa.

skill in means · 方便 fāng biàn · BDK p. 5 expedient means · upāya
6. Attainment
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Sixth, greatness of attainment. One attains immeasurably many great qualities, including the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and qualities unique to a buddha.

7. Activity
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Seventh, greatness of activity. For as long as saṃsāra lasts one displays the attainment of awakening and all the other [deeds of a buddha], carrying out the vast work of the buddhas.”

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

(Of these, the first five are causes and the last two their fruits.)

2. Seven kinds of greatness in the Treatise Expounding the Sacred Teaching
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Second, the Treatise Expounding the Sacred Teaching says, “As for the nature of the Great Vehicle, the bodhisattva vehicle is called ‘great’ because it possesses seven kinds of greatness. What are the seven?

1. Teaching
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

First, greatness of Dharma. Of the twelve divisions of teaching, this means the extensive teaching of skillful means contained in the bodhisattva collection.

2. Aspiration
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Second, greatness of aspiration. One has aroused the aspiration to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

3. Resolute understanding
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Third, greatness of resolute understanding. The great Dharma just described is the object in which one gains firm conviction and understanding.

4. Intention
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Fourth, greatness of intention. One has passed beyond the ground of practice based on resolute understanding and entered the ground of purified higher intention.

5. Requisites
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Fifth, greatness of the requisites. Having fully accumulated the two great requisites, merit and wisdom, one can realize unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

6. Time
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Sixth, greatness of time. Over three incalculable periods of great eons one can realize unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

7. Fulfillment
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Seventh, greatness of fulfillment. This is unsurpassed, perfect awakening itself. Take the very nature of this awakening brought to fulfillment. Among all other things brought to fulfillment, none equals it in its very nature. How much less could any surpass it?”

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

The Yogācārabhūmi and the Treatise on the Bodhisattva Grounds give the same account. The Yogācārabhūmi says, “Of these, the six that run from greatness of Dharma through greatness of time are all causes of the greatness of complete realization. The greatness of complete realization is the fruit of the preceding six kinds of greatness.”

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

My explanation is that although both accounts distinguish seven kinds of greatness, each sets them out with a different purpose. Examination will reveal the purpose in each case. This concludes the explanation of “Great Vehicle.”

2. Awakening faith

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

As for “awakening faith,” the words of this treatise arouse faith in sentient beings. Hence the expression “awakening faith.” “Faith” expresses a settled conviction that something is so. It means confidence that the principle truly exists, ↓ that practice makes realization possible, ↓ and that this realization has inexhaustible virtues. ↓

1. Faith in greatness of essence
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Here, confidence that the principle truly exists is faith in greatness of essence. † Since one trusts that no dharma can be apprehended, one thereby trusts in the reality of the dharma realm in its equality.

greatness of essence · 體大 tǐ dà · BDK p. 8 the “greatness” of the essence
2. Faith in greatness of characteristics
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Confidence that realization is possible is faith in greatness of characteristics. † The virtues inherent in the nature are fully present and perfume sentient beings. † One therefore trusts that this perfuming by its characteristics will surely lead back to the source.

greatness of characteristics · 相大 xiàng dà · BDK p. 8 the “greatness” of the attributes · lakṣaṇa (相)
virtues inherent in the nature · 性功德 xìng gōng dé · BDK p. 8 excellent qualities
3. Faith in greatness of activity
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Confidence that the virtues are inexhaustible in their activity is faith in greatness of activity, † for there is nothing it cannot accomplish.

greatness of activity · 用大 yòng dà · BDK p. 8 the “greatness” of the influences · BDK supplies kriyā for 用 on p. 7.
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

A person who arouses these three kinds of faith can enter the Buddha’s Dharma, cultivate virtues, escape the domain of the Māras, and reach the unsurpassed path. As a sūtra says in verse, “Faith is the source of the path, the mother of virtues. It nourishes every root of goodness, † dispels every doubt and perplexity, and discloses the unsurpassed path. Through faith one may pass beyond the domains of the Māras. Faith reveals the unsurpassed path of liberation. It is the indestructible seed of every virtue, from which the tree of unsurpassed awakening grows.” Faith has immeasurably many virtues such as these. Since one can arouse the aspiration through this treatise, the title speaks of “awakening faith.”

root of goodness · 善根 shàn gēn · BDK p. 5 capacity for goodness · kuśalamūla

3. Treatise

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

As for “treatise,” its wording establishes and settles questions and can serve as a guide. It distinguishes and explains the profound principles governing the characteristics of dharmas. It is this work of discernment that earns it the name “treatise.”

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Taking the title as a whole, the Great Vehicle is the treatise’s guiding theme and essence. Awakening faith is what the treatise is especially able to do. Essence and function are named together in the title, hence “Treatise on Awakening Faith in the Great Vehicle.” †

Treatise on Awakening Faith in the Great Vehicle · 大乘起信論 dà shèng qǐ xìn lùn · BDK p. 1 THE AWAKENING OF FAITH
Wŏnhyo · Separate NotesT1845 ↗
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

I shall explain this treatise under two headings. First I set out the overall purport of the treatise. ↓ Then I work through its meaning by following the text. ↓

1. The overall purport of the treatise

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

As to its overall purport, consider the Buddha Way as a way. How hushed, empty and still! How deep and unfathomable! Profound beyond profundity, it exceeds all appearances. Still beyond stillness, it is present even in the debates of the hundred schools. Though it is nowhere outside appearances, even the five eyes cannot see its body. Though it is right there in words, even the four kinds of eloquence cannot describe what it is like.

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Call it great? It enters even what has no inside, leaving nothing out. Call it minute? It encompasses what has no outside, with room to spare. Shall we say it exists? Through it, even the one suchness is empty. Shall we say it does not exist? Through it, the myriad things come into being. Unable to say what it is, I am driven to call it “the Way.”

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

As for its essence, it is as open as space, with no partiality, and as boundless as the great ocean, utterly impartial. In its utter impartiality it allows both movement and stillness to take effect. In its freedom from partiality, defilement and purity merge. Because defilement and purity merge, ultimate and conventional truth are equal. Because movement and stillness each take effect, there are different degrees of ascent and descent. Because ascent and descent differ, beings can call forth a response. Because ultimate and conventional truth are equal, there is no way to approach it by thought or discussion.

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Where thought and discussion end, whoever embodies the Way moves freely with its reflections and echoes. Because an appeal can meet with a response, whoever calls upon it goes beyond names and characteristics and finds a refuge. The reflections and echoes it sends forth have neither shape nor speech. Once beyond names and characteristics, what does one go beyond, and to what does one return? This is called the ultimate principle of no principle, the great “so” of “not so.” Apart from the bodhisattva who kept silence and the man who understood at a glance, who could discourse on the Great Vehicle where there is no vehicle, † or awaken deep faith where there is no faith?

Great Vehicle · 大乘 dà shèng · BDK p. 3 Mahayana · Mahāyāna
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Thus the bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, in great compassion that takes nothing as its object, grieved to see how readily beings are swept away when the delusive wind of ignorance stirs the ocean of mind. † He took pity on them, for their true nature, original awakening, sleeps a long dream from which it is hard to wake. † Through the power of the wisdom that sees a common essence, he was able to compose this treatise to expound the profound import of the Tathāgata’s deep sūtras. He wanted students, on briefly opening one scroll, to gather the purport of all three baskets, and followers of the Way to let the myriad objects of experience rest for good and so return to the source, the One Mind.

ignorance · 無明 wú míng · BDK p. 25 nonenlightenment (avidyā) · avidyā · Hakeda usually calls 無明 ‘ignorance’. His parallel here pairs 無明 with 無漏.
original awakening · 本覺 běn jué · BDK p. 17 original enlightenment
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

As a treatise, it leaves nothing unaffirmed and nothing unrefuted. Works such as the Treatise on the Middle and the Treatise on the Twelve Gates refute every position one can cling to and even refute refutation itself. They do not, in turn, admit either what does the refuting or what is refuted. We may say that such treatises go forth without covering the whole ground.⁕

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Works such as the Yogācārabhūmi and the Compendium of the Mahāyāna set out both profound and elementary teachings and distinguish their approaches to the Dharma. Yet they do not dissolve and relinquish the dharmas they themselves establish. We may say that such treatises grant without taking away.

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

The present treatise displays both wisdom and benevolence. It is profound and also communicates that profundity.⁕ It affirms everything, then relinquishes its own affirmations. It refutes everything, then admits again what it refuted. By admitting it again, it shows how refutation, taken to its furthest reach, affirms on every side. By relinquishing its affirmations, it shows how granting, carried to its limit, takes away. Hence we may call it the ancestor of the treatises and the arbiter of their many disputes.

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Although the treatise ranges widely, its argument can be put briefly. By opening two gateways within the One Mind, † it encompasses the extensive teaching on the hundred and eight [questions of the Laṅkāvatāra] on Mount Malaya. By displaying purity of nature within defilement of characteristics, it gathers up the profound import of the fifteen [chapters of the Śrīmālā Sūtra] at Ayodhyā.

two gateways · 二門 èr mén · BDK p. 11 two aspects
BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Consider also the doctrine of a single taste at the Crane Grove [where the Buddha entered final nirvāṇa], the nondual purport of the teaching on Vulture Peak, the three bodies as the ultimate fruit in the Golden Drum and the Same Nature, the four stages as profound causes in the Flower Garland and the Jeweled Necklace, the vast and open supreme Way in the Large Perfection of Wisdom and the Great Collection, and the hidden, profound gateways of the Sun Treasury and the Moon Treasury. What runs a single thread through the heart of all these scriptures? Can it be anything but this treatise? Hence the text says below, “To gather together the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma, one should expound this treatise.”

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

The words of the treatise are close at hand, yet its principle reaches far. Its text is short, yet its meanings are many. Few who have explained it have grasped its central teaching. Each holds fast to what he has learned and strains the text to fit it, unable to approach its meaning with an open mind. Thus they come nowhere near the author’s intent. One looks toward the source but describes the stream. Another grasps a leaf and calls it the trunk. One cuts off the collar to mend the sleeve. Another breaks off a stick and drags the root along with it.

BDK p. 1 ↗Title · introductory exposition

Here I simply follow the text of this treatise and match its passages to the sūtras they expound. I give the main points in outline and record them for my own use. I do not presume to hope that they will be disseminated throughout the world. This concludes the account of the treatise’s overall purport.

Taking refuge in the Three Jewels

Invocation

p. 3 I take refuge in [the Buddha,]⁕ the greatly Compassionate One, the savior of the world, omnipotent, omnipresent, omniscient, of most excellent deeds in all the ten directions;

p. 3 And in [the Dharma, the manifestation of his essence,⁕ the reality, the sea of suchness, the boundless storehouse of excellencies;⁕

p. 3 [And in the Sangha, whose members] truly devote themselves to the practice,

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

3. Interpreting the wording of the treatise

BDK p. 3 ↗I take refuge in [the Buddha,]

Third, to interpret the text. It has three divisions. First come three stanzas expressing homage and the author's intention. ↓ From “The treatise says” onward, he sets out the body of the treatise. ↓ In the last stanza he concludes and dedicates the merit.

1. Homage and intention

BDK p. 3 ↗I take refuge in [the Buddha,]

The opening three stanzas serve two purposes. With the first two the author takes refuge in the Three Jewels. ↓ In the last he states his intention in writing the treatise. ↓

1. Taking refuge in the Three Jewels
BDK p. 3 ↗I take refuge in [the Buddha,]

The opening homage has two parts. The two characters “entrust my life” describe the act of taking refuge. † ↓ From “throughout the ten directions” onward, he sets forth the virtues of those in whom he takes refuge. † ↓

entrust my life · 歸命 guī mìng · BDK p. 3 I take refuge
throughout the ten directions · 盡十方 jìn shí fāng · BDK p. 3 in all the ten directions
1. The act of taking refuge
BDK p. 3 ↗I take refuge in [the Buddha,]

As for the act itself, “to take refuge” (歸) means to follow reverently. It also means to turn toward. “Life” (命) means the life faculty, which governs all the faculties together. Of everything essential to the body, life is chief. Of all that living beings cherish, nothing comes before it. To offer the one life one has in homage to the supremely honored one expresses faith at its utmost. Hence “I entrust my life.” “Entrusting one's life” also means returning to the source. Why? Beings’ six sense faculties arise from the one mind, yet turn their backs on their source and scatter in pursuit of the six sense objects. Here, in offering one's life, one gathers the six faculties together and returns to their source, the one mind. Hence “I entrust my life.” For the one mind to which one returns is itself the Three Jewels.

2. The virtues of those in whom refuge is taken
BDK p. 3 ↗of most excellent deeds in all the ten directions;

From “throughout the ten directions” onward he sets forth the virtues of those in whom he takes refuge. This would be the place to explain the Three Jewels. Their meaning is discussed elsewhere. Here I shall simply explain the wording. The text has three parts, one for each jewel, Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. ↓ ↓ ↓

1. The Buddha
BDK p. 3 ↗of most excellent deeds in all the ten directions;

Within [the first] there are three points. First he praises the virtues of mind, then the virtues of form. ↓ ↓ In the third line he concludes the praise by naming the person. ↓

1. Virtues of mind
BDK p. 3 ↗of most excellent deeds in all the ten directions;

In praising the virtues of mind, he praises its activity and its essence. ↓ ↓

1. Activity
BDK p. 3 ↗of most excellent deeds in all the ten directions;

The opening words “supreme deeds throughout the ten directions” praise the Buddha's activity. † These are the deeds by which he teaches beings, such as manifesting the eight events [of a buddha's life]. They extend to every world in the ten directions and throughout past, present, and future. In response to those ready to receive instruction, he does the work of a buddha. Hence “supreme deeds throughout the ten directions.” As the Abhidharma treatise says, “Greatness of activity means that for as long as saṃsāra lasts, one manifests the attainment of awakening and all the other [events of buddhahood], thereby undertaking the vast work of the buddhas.” That text speaks of the three times. This one speaks of the ten directions.

supreme deeds · 最勝業 zuì shèng yè · BDK p. 3 of most excellent deeds
2. Wisdom itself
BDK p. 3 ↗omniscient,

“All-pervading wisdom” praises wisdom itself. † His activity extends throughout the ten directions because there is nowhere that wisdom itself does not reach. Because wisdom itself pervades everything, he calls it “all-pervading wisdom.” The Compendium of the Great Vehicle says, “Just as space extends as far as form extends, without arising, abiding, ceasing, or changing, so the Tathāgata's wisdom extends to all that can be known, free from distortion and change.” This completes the praise of the virtues of mind.

All-pervading wisdom · 遍智 biàn zhì · BDK p. 3 omniscient · Wŏnhyo quotes 遍智, while T1666 reads 遍知.
2. Virtues of form
BDK p. 3 ↗omnipotent, omnipresent,

Next he praises the virtues of form, again in two parts. “Unobstructed form” praises the subtle excellence of form itself. † ↓ “Mastery” praises its extraordinary activity. † ↓

Unobstructed form · 色無礙 sè wú ài · BDK p. 3 omnipotent, omnipresent · Hakeda renders 色無礙自在 as a unit.
Mastery · 自在 zì zài · BDK p. 3 omnipotent, omnipresent · Hakeda renders 色無礙自在 as a unit.
1. Form itself
BDK p. 3 ↗omnipotent, omnipresent,

As to form itself, the myriad practices bring the Tathāgata's physical body to perfection, as does inconceivable perfuming. Though endowed with wondrous form, it is free of obstruction. Every major and minor bodily characteristic is without bound or limit. Hence the words “unobstructed form.” The Flower Garland Sūtra says, “One might yet find the limit of space, but a single pore of the Buddha has no bound. So inconceivable are a buddha's virtues. This is called the Tathāgata's pure knowledge and vision.” Though it presents no material obstruction, it can appear in a particular place. It can therefore be called form and still be unobstructed.

2. The activity of form
BDK p. 3 ↗omnipotent, omnipresent,

“Mastery” praises the activity of his form. The five sense faculties can each perform the others’ functions, the ten bodies can each become the others, and so forth. Hence “mastery of form.”

BDK p. 3 ↗omnipotent, omnipresent,

The Nirvāṇa Sūtra explains the interchange of the five faculties in its account of the eight masteries. The Flower Garland Sūtra explains the interchange of the ten bodies in its chapter on the Ten Grounds. This completes the praise of the virtues of form.

3. The person praised
BDK p. 3 ↗the greatly Compassionate One, the savior of the world,

“The one of great compassion who saves the world” is the third line, which concludes the praise by naming the person. † The Buddha is like a wealthy elder who regards sentient beings as his children. He enters the burning house of the three realms to rescue them from the anguish of the flames. Hence “saves the world.” The virtue by which he saves the world is precisely great compassion. Free of the distinction between self and other, compassion that takes no object is supreme among forms of compassion. Hence “great compassion.” Of the myriad virtues of the buddha stage, great compassion alone is the Tathāgata's strength. He singles it out to indicate who the Buddha is. As the Numerical Āgama says, “Ordinary beings and sages have six kinds of strength. Which six? A little child's strength is crying. To express a wish, it must first cry. A woman's strength is anger. She first gives way to anger and then says what she has to say. The strength of ascetics and brahmins is patience. They are always mindful to put themselves below others before speaking for themselves. A king's strength is pride. He speaks for himself with the authority of his rank. An arhat speaks for himself with the strength of single-minded application. The strength of the buddhas, the world-honored ones, is great compassion, for they bring far-reaching benefit to beings.” From this we know that great compassion in particular is the buddhas’ strength. To identify the person, then, the verse calls him “the one of great compassion.” The preceding three lines complete the praise of the Buddha Jewel.

The one of great compassion who saves the world · 救世大悲者 jiù shì dà bēi zhě · BDK p. 3 the greatly Compassionate One, the savior of the world · mahākaruṇā (大悲)
2. The Dharma
BDK p. 3 ↗And in [the Dharma, the manifestation of his essence,

The next two lines disclose the Dharma Jewel. “And the essence and characteristics of his body” refers to the Tathāgata's body just mentioned, the Buddha in his fruition body. † The very essence of that body is the dharma realm. Hence “the essence and characteristics of his body.” Here he refers to the Buddha to indicate his Dharma. The next line directly sets out the essence and characteristics of the Dharma Jewel.

the essence and characteristics of his body · 及彼身體相 jí bǐ shēn tǐ xiàng · BDK p. 3 the manifestation of his essence
1. Dharma-nature
BDK p. 3 ↗the reality, the sea of suchness,

“Dharma-nature” refers to nirvāṇa. † Because it is the fundamental nature of dharmas, it is called “dharma-nature.” As the Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says, “‘Dharma’ means nirvāṇa, the Dharma free of conceptual proliferation. ‘Nature’ means the kind inherent in a thing, like the nature of gold in yellow ore and the nature of silver in white ore.” In this way all dharmas have the nature of nirvāṇa. Hence “dharma-nature.”

Dharma-nature · 法性 fǎ xìng · BDK p. 3 the reality · dharmatā
2. Suchness
BDK p. 3 ↗the reality, the sea of suchness,

In the term “true suchness,” where there is nothing to negate, one says “true” (真), and where there is nothing to posit, one says “such” (如). As the text says below, “In suchness itself there is nothing to negate, since all dharmas are true. There is also nothing to posit, since all dharmas are alike in being such.” Understand that all dharmas are beyond speech and thought. Hence the name “true suchness.”

3. The ocean
BDK p. 3 ↗the reality, the sea of suchness,

With “ocean” he makes the Dharma clear by a simile. Briefly, the ocean suggests four things. First, it is deep. ↓ Second, it is vast. ↓ Third, its treasures are inexhaustible. ↓ Fourth, the images of all things appear reflected in it. ↓ Understand the great ocean of suchness in the same way. It is forever beyond the hundred negations. It encompasses all things. It possesses every virtue. Every image appears in it. Hence “the ocean of dharma-nature, of true suchness.” † The Flower Garland Sūtra says, “As in the deep, vast ocean, whose treasures never run out, images of every shape and kind of being appear, so in the profound ocean of causes and conditions the treasures of virtue are inexhaustible. In the pure Dharma body every image appears.” This completes the praise of the Dharma Jewel.

the ocean of dharma-nature, of true suchness · 真如海 zhēn rú hǎi · BDK p. 3 the sea of suchness · tathatā (真如)
3. The Saṅgha
BDK p. 3 ↗the boundless storehouse of excellencies;

The next two lines praise the Saṅgha Jewel.

1. A treasury of immeasurable virtues
BDK p. 3 ↗the boundless storehouse of excellencies;

“Treasury of immeasurable virtues” names the virtues to indicate the persons who possess them. † These are bodhisattvas who have reached the grounds. In whatever single practice they cultivate, the myriad practices come together and reach fulfillment. Each of their practices is as boundless as the dharma realm. What they gain through accumulated effort is therefore called “immeasurable virtue.” All these virtues belong to the bodhisattvas. Because the persons encompass the virtues, they are called a “treasury.”

Treasury of immeasurable virtues · 無量功德藏 wú liàng gōng dé zàng · BDK p. 3 the boundless storehouse of excellencies · BDK places this line with the Dharma. Wŏnhyo reads it as praise of the Saṅgha.
2. Practicing in accordance with reality
BDK p. 3 ↗[And in the Sangha, whose members] truly devote themselves to the practice,

“Those who practice in accordance with reality, and so forth” directly praises the virtues of their practice. †

practice in accordance with reality · 如實修行 rú shí xiū xíng · BDK p. 3 truly devote themselves to the practice
1. The two wisdoms
BDK p. 3 ↗[And in the Sangha, whose members] truly devote themselves to the practice,

According to the Jewel Lineage Treatise, practice in accordance with reality is named for fundamental wisdom. Subsequently acquired wisdom is called all-embracing practice. Here, “practice in accordance with reality” refers to fundamental wisdom. The following “and so forth” includes subsequently acquired wisdom.

2. Practice and heedfulness
BDK p. 3 ↗[And in the Sangha, whose members] truly devote themselves to the practice,

According to the Dharma Collection Sūtra, the myriad practices, from beginning to end, all fall under two expressions, “practice in accordance with reality” and “heedfulness.” That sūtra says, “‘Practice in accordance with reality’ means making the vow for awakening. ‘Heedfulness’ means fulfilling that vow. Again, ‘practice in accordance with reality’ means practicing generosity. ‘Heedfulness’ means looking for no reward. Likewise, one keeps the precepts pure and attains nonretrogression. † One cultivates patience and gains acceptance of the nonarising [of dharmas]. One pursues all roots of goodness without growing weary. One relinquishes all one's undertakings. One cultivates meditative concentration without settling in it. One brings wisdom to fulfillment without engaging in conceptual proliferation about dharmas. In their respective order these are practice in accordance with reality and heedfulness.” The sūtra explains this at length. Here, “practice in accordance with reality” includes everything from making the vow for awakening through bringing wisdom to fulfillment. The following “and so forth” includes heedfulness, from fulfilling that vow through refraining from conceptual proliferation about dharmas. This completes the foregoing homage to the Three Jewels.

nonretrogression · 不退 bù tuì · BDK p. 5 nonretrogressive faith

BDK p. 3 ↗I take refuge in [the Buddha,]

Second comes the explanation following the text. The wording of the opening homage in verse and of the section on the reasons [for writing] can be understood as it stands. †

section on the reasons · 因緣分 yīn yuán fēn · BDK p. 3 the Reasons for Writing

The purpose of the invocation

p. 3 May all sentient beings be made to discard their doubts, cast aside their evil attachments, and give rise to the correct faith in the Mahayana, that the lineage of the Buddhas may not be broken off.

3. Interpreting the wording of the treatise

1. Homage and intention

3. Interpreting the wording of the treatise › 1. Homage and intention

2. The author's intention
BDK p. 3 ↗May all sentient beings be made

The following stanza gives the author's overall intention in writing the treatise.

BDK p. 3 ↗May all sentient beings be made

His purpose in writing the treatise is twofold. The first half of the stanza explains how he reaches down to teach sentient beings. ↓ The second shows how he looks upward to carry forward the Buddha's path. ↓

1. Teaching sentient beings
BDK p. 3 ↗to discard their doubts,

Why have beings long been submerged in the ocean of birth and death, without making for the shore of nirvāṇa? Simply because of their doubts and mistaken attachments. † To teach beings, then, the essential thing is to enable them to dispel doubt and abandon mistaken attachments. ↓ ↓

mistaken attachments · 邪執 xié zhí · BDK p. 3 evil attachments
1. Dispelling doubt
BDK p. 3 ↗to discard their doubts,

Doubts generally take many forms. Those who seek the Great Vehicle face two. First, doubt about the Dharma keeps one from arousing the aspiration for awakening. ↓ Second, doubt about the gateways keeps one from practicing. ↓

1. Doubt about the Dharma
BDK p. 3 ↗to discard their doubts,

To doubt the Dharma is to wonder whether the essence of the Dharma of the Great Vehicle is one or many. If it is one, there are no distinct dharmas. If there are no distinct dharmas, there are no distinct beings. For whom, then, would a bodhisattva make the vast vow? If there are many dharmas, they do not share a single essence. Without a single essence, others and I are separate. How could great compassion born of sharing one essence arise? Doubting in this way, one cannot arouse the aspiration.

2. Doubt about the gateways
BDK p. 3 ↗to discard their doubts,

One who doubts the gateways reasons, “The Tathāgata has established many gateways in his teaching. Which one should I rely on to begin practicing? If I should rely on all of them together, I cannot enter them all at once. If I should rely on one or two, which should I set aside and which take up?” Doubting in this way, one cannot begin to practice.

3. How the treatise resolves the two doubts
BDK p. 3 ↗to discard their doubts,

To dispel these two doubts, the author sets forth the Dharma of the one mind and opens two gateways. ↓ ↓

1. The one mind
BDK p. 3 ↗to discard their doubts,

Setting forth the Dharma of the one mind dispels the first doubt. He shows that the Dharma of the Great Vehicle is simply the one mind. Outside that mind there are no other dharmas. It is only through ignorance that one loses sight of one's own one mind, stirring up waves and wandering through the six destinies. Although the waves of the six destinies rise up, they never leave the ocean of the one mind. Precisely because the one mind stirs and becomes the six destinies, one can make the vast vow to rescue beings. Because the six destinies never leave the one mind, great compassion born of sharing one essence can arise. With doubt dispelled in this way, one can arouse the great aspiration.

2. The two gateways
BDK p. 3 ↗to discard their doubts,

Opening two gateways dispels the second doubt. He shows that, however many gateways the teachings provide, all entry into practice comes through these two. Relying on the gateway of suchness, one cultivates tranquility (śamatha). † Relying on the gateway of arising and ceasing, one develops insight (vipaśyanā). † With tranquility and insight working together, all the myriad practices are complete. † In entering these two gateways, one gains access to them all. With doubt dispelled in this way, one can begin to practice.

gateway of suchness · 真如門 zhēn rú mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of the absolute
gateway of arising and ceasing · 生滅門 shēng miè mén · BDK p. 11 aspect of Mind in terms of phenomena
tranquility and insight · 止觀 zhǐ guān · BDK p. 5 cessation [of illusions] and clear observation · śamatha and vipaśyanā
2. Abandoning mistaken attachments
BDK p. 3 ↗cast aside their evil attachments,

“Abandon mistaken attachments” refers to two kinds of attachment, grasping at persons and grasping at dharmas. How one abandons these two will be explained below. This completes the explanation of teaching sentient beings.

2. Carrying forward the Buddha's path
BDK p. 3 ↗and give rise to the correct faith in the Mahayana,

The next two lines deal with carrying forward the Buddha's path. When doubts about the two extremes have been dispelled, settled faith can arise. One has faith in and understands the Great Vehicle as simply the one mind. Hence “arouse right faith in the Great Vehicle.” †

right faith · 正信 zhèng xìn · BDK p. 3 correct faith
BDK p. 3 ↗that the lineage of the Buddhas may not be broken off.

Giving up the discriminations involved in the two attachments just mentioned, one gains nondiscriminating wisdom, is born into the Tathāgata's family, and can succeed to the rank of a buddha. Hence “so that the buddha lineage will continue unbroken.” † As a treatise says, “Through faith one can enter the great ocean of the Buddha-Dharma. Through wisdom one can cross it.” He therefore speaks of faith and wisdom to show how one carries forward the Buddha's path. The stanza opens with “in order to” (為) and closes with “for this purpose” (故), making clear the two purposes for which he wrote this treatise. This completes the homage and statement of intention.

buddha lineage · 佛種 fó zhǒng · BDK p. 3 lineage of the Buddhas
BDK p. 3

The five parts of the treatise

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda
The Contents of the Discourse

p. 3 There is a teaching (Dharma) that can awaken in us the root of faith in the Mahayana, and it should therefore be explained. The explanation is divided into five parts. They are 1) the Reasons for Writing; 2) the Outline; 3) the Interpretation; 4) on Faith and Practice; 5) the Encouragement of Practice and the Benefits Thereof.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

Body of the treatise

BDK p. 3 ↗There is a teaching (Dharma)

Here begins the second main division, in which the author presents the body of the treatise. The text has three parts. First, he announces what he proposes to explain. ↓ Second, he gives the number of parts and names them. ↓ Third, he explains each part in turn. ↓ Their places in the text are evident.

1. The promise to explain

BDK p. 3 ↗There is a teaching (Dharma)

In the first part, “there is a dharma” means the dharma of the one mind. Whoever understands this dharma will surely develop a far-reaching faculty of faith. † Hence “it can give rise to the faculty of faith in the Great Vehicle.” I explained the characteristics of this faculty when discussing the title. Once the faculty of faith is established, one enters the path to Buddhahood. Having entered that path, one obtains inexhaustible treasure. Such great benefit comes by way of this treatise. That is why the author should expound it. This completes the general announcement of what he proposes to explain.

faculty of faith · 信根 xìn gēn · BDK p. 3 root of faith · śraddhendriya

2. The five divisions

BDK p. 3 ↗The explanation is divided into five parts.

“The explanation has five parts” begins the second part, numbering and naming the divisions. “There are five parts” gives their number. From “What are they?” he lists their names.

1. Reasons for writing
BDK p. 3 ↗1) the Reasons for Writing;

“Causes and conditions.” The author had grounds for undertaking the treatise. † ↓ One should first know what a wise person intends by such an undertaking.

Causes and conditions · 因緣分 yīn yuán fēn · BDK p. 3 the Reasons for Writing
2. Establishing the meaning
BDK p. 3 ↗2) the Outline;

“Establishing the meaning.” Once he has given his reasons, he should set out the correct meaning. † ↓ Without a brief statement, one would miss the essential point.

Establishing the meaning · 立義分 lì yì fēn · BDK p. 3 the Outline
3. Explanation
BDK p. 3 ↗3) the Interpretation;

“Explanation.” Having stated his main point briefly, he should now discuss it at length. † Without this exposition the meaning would be hard to grasp.

Explanation · 解釋分 jiě shì fēn · BDK p. 3 the Interpretation
4. Cultivating faith
BDK p. 3 ↗4) on Faith and Practice;

“Cultivating faith.” Once the explanation has given rise to faith, one must go on to practice. † Understanding without practice falls short of the treatise’s intent.

Cultivating faith · 修行信心分 xiū xíng xìn xīn fēn · BDK p. 3 on Faith and Practice
5. Benefits that encourage practice
BDK p. 3 ↗5) the Encouragement of Practice and the Benefits Thereof.

“Benefits that encourage practice.” Even after being shown how to cultivate faith, † people whose roots of goodness are weak are reluctant to undertake the practice. So the author sets out its benefits to urge them to take it up. Hence the title “Benefits that encourage practice.”

Benefits that encourage practice · 勸修利益分 quàn xiū lì yì fēn · BDK p. 3 the Encouragement of Practice and the Benefits Thereof
BDK pp. 5–6

Eight reasons for writing

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda
Part One

p. 5 The Reasons for Writing

p. 5 Someone may ask the reasons why I was led to write this treatise. I reply: there are eight reasons.

p. 5 The first and the main reason is to cause human beings to free themselves from all suffering and to gain the final bliss; it is not that I desire worldly fame, material profit, or respect and honor.

p. 5 The second reason is that I wish to interpret the fundamental meaning [of the teachings] of the Tathāgata so that people may understand them correctly and not be mistaken about them.

p. 5 The third reason is to enable those whose capacity for goodness has attained maturity to keep firm hold upon a nonretrogressive faith in the teachings of the Mahayana.

p. 5 The fourth reason is to encourage those whose capacity for goodness is still slight to cultivate the faithful mind.

p. 5 The fifth reason is to show them expedient means (upāya) by which they may wipe away the hindrance of evil karma, guard their minds well, free themselves from stupidity and arrogance, and escape from the net of heresy.

p. 5 The sixth reason is to reveal to them the practice [of two methods of meditation], cessation [of illusions] and clear observation (śamatha and vipaśyanā; Ch., zhiguan), so that ordinary people and the followers of the Hinayana may cure their minds of error.⁕

p. 5–6 The seventh reason is to explain to them the expedient means of singleminded meditation (smṛti) so that they may be born in the presence of the Buddha and keep their minds fixed in a nonretrogressive faith.

p. 6 The eighth reason is to point out to them the advantage [of studying this treatise] and to encourage them to make an effort [to attain enlightenment]. These are the reasons for which I write this treatise.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

Body of the treatise

Body of the treatise

3. Explanation by division

BDK p. 5 ↗The Reasons for Writing

The third part, explaining the divisions in turn, thus has five parts.

I. Reasons for writing
BDK p. 5 ↗The Reasons for Writing

The first has two parts. The author first repeats the heading, then gives his reasons. In giving his reasons he uses two questions and answers. The first states the reasons directly. The second resolves a doubt. ↓ ↓

1. Direct statement
BDK p. 5 ↗Someone may ask the reasons why I was led to write this treatise.

The first question is self-explanatory. The answer opens with a general statement, explains the reasons individually, and ends by drawing them together. ↓ ↓

Individual reasons
BDK p. 5 ↗I reply: there are eight reasons.

In the second part, which explains the eight reasons individually, the first is a general reason and the remaining seven are specific. ↓ ↓

1. A general reason
BDK p. 5 ↗The first and the main reason

The first is called general in two senses. ↓ ↓

1. Common to bodhisattvas’ undertakings
BDK p. 5 ↗is to cause human beings to free themselves from all suffering and to gain the final bliss;

First, whenever bodhisattvas undertake anything, they do so for beings to escape suffering and find happiness. This motive extends beyond the composition of the present treatise. In that sense it is general.

2. Common to the divisions of this work
BDK p. 5 ↗The first and the main reason

Second, although this reason serves specifically as the condition for the division establishing the meaning, that division provides the common basis for the explanation and the remaining divisions. This reason therefore serves as a condition for them all. In that sense too it is general.

BDK p. 5 ↗is to cause human beings to free themselves from all suffering and to gain the final bliss;

“To escape all suffering” includes all the suffering both of birth and death in distinct lifetimes and of birth and death through subtle transformation. “Ultimate happiness” is the happiness of unsurpassed awakening and great nirvāṇa. † “Without seeking worldly rewards” means having no expectation of wealth and pleasure as a human or a deva in a future life. “Fame, gain, and honor” means the hollow things of this life, which the author does not seek.

Ultimate happiness · 究竟樂 jiū jìng lè · BDK p. 5 the final bliss
BDK p. 5 ↗The second reason is that I wish to interpret the fundamental meaning [of the teachings]…

The next seven are specific reasons. They are peculiar to the composition of this treatise, and each serves as the condition for a particular passage among seven that follow.

2. Explaining the Tathāgata’s fundamental meaning
BDK p. 5 ↗The second reason is that I wish to interpret the fundamental meaning [of the teachings]…

The second reason accounts for two of the three sections within the division of explanation, namely, revealing the correct meaning and counteracting mistaken attachments. ↓ ↓ The section revealing the correct meaning says, “On the basis of the dharma of the one mind there are two gateways. Each of these gateways encompasses all dharmas.” Understand that this is the fundamental meaning of all the gateways to Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.

BDK p. 5 ↗so that people may understand them correctly and not be mistaken about them.

The two gateways of this one mind encompass every dharma and every meaning. Hence “in order to explain the Tathāgata’s fundamental meaning.” The second section, counteracting mistaken attachments, leads beings to relinquish both mistaken attachment to persons and mistaken attachment to dharmas. Hence “so that beings may understand correctly and without error.”

3. Bringing mature faith to nonretrogression
BDK p. 5 ↗The third reason is to enable those whose capacity for goodness has attained maturity

The third reason accounts for the third section within the division of explanation. That section distinguishes the ways one sets out upon and advances along the path. It enables those with sharp faculties to resolve firmly upon awakening and advance along the great path, † until they are capable of abiding at the stage of nonretrogression. Hence “so that those whose roots of goodness … [may attain] faith that does not regress.”

sharp faculties · 利根 lì gēn · BDK p. 6 high aptitude
4. Cultivating faith
BDK p. 5 ↗The fourth reason is to encourage those whose capacity for goodness is still slight

The fourth reason accounts for the four kinds of faith and the four practices set out at the beginning of the division on cultivating faith. Hence “to enable them to cultivate faith.”

5. Removing karmic obstructions
BDK p. 5 ↗The fifth reason is to show them expedient means (upāya)

The fifth reason accounts for the passage at the end of the fourth practice that begins, “Furthermore, someone may cultivate faith yet carry many grave obstructions from unskillful karma accumulated in past lives.” † In the next five lines or so, the author teaches a way to remove these obstructions. Hence “to show skillful means to remove the obstructions of unskillful karma … and escape the net of wrong views.” †

obstructions from unskillful karma · 惡業障 è yè zhàng · BDK p. 5 the hindrance of evil karma · karmāvaraṇa (業障)
net of wrong views · 邪網 xié wǎng · BDK p. 5 net of heresy
6. Tranquility and insight
BDK p. 5 ↗The sixth reason is to reveal to them the practice [of two methods of meditation],…

The sixth reason accounts for about three sheets of text, from “How does one cultivate tranquility and insight?” through “without both tranquility and insight, one cannot enter the path to awakening.” Hence “cultivate tranquility and insight … [to remedy] faults of mind.”

7. Recollection and rebirth in a pure land
BDK p. 5–6 ↗The seventh reason is to explain to them the expedient means of singleminded meditation (smṛti)

The seventh reason corresponds to “Furthermore, beings who are beginning to learn this Dharma” at the end of the division on cultivating faith. The passage that follows, about eight lines long, encourages them to seek rebirth in a pure land. Hence “to show the skillful means of single-minded recollection for rebirth in a buddha’s presence,” and so on. † †

single-minded recollection · 專念 zhuān niàn · BDK p. 5–6 singleminded meditation · BDK supplies smṛti for recollection (念).
rebirth in a buddha’s presence · 生於佛前 shēng yú fó qián · BDK p. 5–6 born in the presence of the Buddha
8. Encouraging practice
BDK p. 6 ↗The eighth reason is to point out to them the advantage [of studying this treatise]

The eighth reason accounts for the treatise’s fifth division, which sets out the benefits to encourage practice. Hence “to show the benefits and encourage practice.”

The concluding statement
BDK p. 6 ↗These are the reasons for which I write this treatise.

The next words, “It is for reasons such as these that I compose the treatise,” form the third part, the general conclusion. This completes the direct statement of the reasons.

BDK p. 6

Why write a treatise after the sūtras?

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 6 Question: What need is there to repeat the explanation of the teaching when it is presented in detail in the sutras?

p. 6 Answer: Though this teaching is presented in the sutras, the capacity and the deeds of people today are no longer the same, nor are the conditions of their acceptance and comprehension. That is to say, in the days when the Tathāgata was in the world, people were of high aptitude and the Preacher excelled in his form, mind, and deeds, so that once he had preached with his perfect voice, different types of people all equally understood; hence, there was no need for this kind of discourse.

p. 6 But after the passing away of the Tathāgata, there were some who were able by their own power to listen extensively to others and to reach understanding; there were some who by their own power could listen to very little and yet understand much; there were some who, without an mental power of their own,⁕ depended upon the extensive discourses of others to obtain understanding; and naturally there were some who looked upon the wordiness of extensive discourses as troublesome, and who sought after what was comprehensive, terse, and yet contained much meaning, and then were able to understand it.

p. 6 Thus, this discourse is designed to embrace, in a general way, the limitless meaning of the vast and profound teaching of the Tathāgata. This discourse, therefore, should be presented.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

Body of the treatise

3. Explanation by division

I. Reasons for writing

Body of the treatise › 3. Explanation by division › I. Reasons for writing

2. Resolving a doubt
BDK p. 6 ↗Question:

The following passage resolves a doubt by posing a question and answering it. ↓ ↓

The question
BDK p. 6 ↗of the teaching when it is presented in detail in the sutras?

In the question, “the sūtras already teach this Dharma in full” refers to everything taught on the basis of the eight reasons, from the dharma and its meaning set out in the outline right through to the benefits described in the exhortation to practice. The sūtras teach all these dharmas in full so that beings may escape suffering and find happiness. If one now composes a treatise to repeat these teachings, can one really be seeking anything other than fame, gain, or the like? “Why explain them again?” voices this doubt as a question.

The answer
BDK p. 6 ↗Answer:

The answer has three parts. A brief reply is followed by a detailed explanation and finally a short conclusion. ↓ ↓ ↓

1. Brief reply
BDK p. 6 ↗Though this teaching is presented in the sutras,

“Although the sūtras teach this Dharma” grants the premise of the question. “Faculties and ways of practice differ, and so do the conditions under which people receive and understand the teaching” takes away the grounds for doubt. † Sūtras and treatises teach the same Dharma. Those who receive and understand it differ in their faculties and ways of practice. Some can rely on sūtras and have no need of treatises. Others can rely on treatises and have no need of sūtras. For the latter a treatise must be written. This is what the reply means.

Faculties and ways of practice · 根行 gēn xíng · BDK p. 6 the capacity and the deeds
2. Detailed explanation
BDK p. 6 ↗That is to say, in the days when the Tathāgata was in the world,

The detailed explanation has two parts. The first describes the excellence of both speaker and listeners during the Buddha’s lifetime. ↓ The second shows how faculties and conditions varied after the Tathāgata’s passing. ↓

1. During the Buddha’s lifetime
BDK p. 6 ↗people were of high aptitude

In the first part, “while the Tathāgata was in the world, beings had sharp faculties” shows the excellence of the listeners. “The speaker excelled in bodily form, mind, and activity” shows the excellence of the speaker. † “In a single utterance of his perfect voice” bears out the speaker’s excellence. “Different kinds of beings all understood” bears out the listeners’ excellence. “There was then no need for a treatise” draws the conclusion from the excellence of both.

excelled in bodily form, mind, and activity · 色心業勝 sè xīn yè shèng · BDK p. 6 excelled in his form, mind, and deeds
The Buddha’s one perfect voice
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

The “perfect voice” here is the “one voice.” In what sense is the voice one, and in what sense perfect? Teachers have long differed in their explanations. ↓ ↓ ↓

1. Like the echo in an empty valley
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

One teacher says, “Buddhas are solely the body of ultimate truth, forever beyond all appearances, without form or sound. In response to beings’ capacities they manifest boundless visible forms and sounds, just as a valley empty of sound gives back an echo in response to a call.” On this account, from the Buddha’s side the oneness consists in the absence of sound. From the side of beings’ capacities there are many distinct sounds. Why, then, call the voice one and perfect? Because at one time in one assembly, beings of different kinds all understand. Each receives one sound suited to their faculties and disposition and hears no other. There is neither confusion nor mistake. This extraordinary quality earns it the name “one voice.” The voice reaches the ten directions. Wherever a being’s capacity has ripened, it can be heard. Hence “perfect voice.” This does not mean a voice that fills everything like space and lacks distinct tones or melodies. This is what the sūtra means by “He addresses all beings in the sounds proper to their kind.”

2. Like the moon reflected in many vessels
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

Another account holds that, from the Buddha’s side, there really are visible form and sound. His voice is complete and reaches everywhere. It contains no distinctions of musical pitch such as gōng and shāng. How could it have such distinctions of speech as the level and rising tones? It is called “one voice” because it has no different melodies, and “perfect voice” because it reaches everywhere. This perfect voice acts as a predominant condition. Many distinct sounds manifest according to differences in beings’ faculties, just as the full moon has a single round form yet appears in many reflections according to the vessels that reflect it. Understand the principle here in the same way. For the sūtra says, “The Buddha teaches the Dharma in one voice, and beings each understand according to their kind.”

3. All voices in one
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

Another account holds that the Tathāgata really has many voices. Every sound uttered by any being is included in the sound of the Tathāgata turning the wheel of Dharma. The Buddha’s voice is free of every obstruction. One is all, and all are one. Since all are one, it is called “one voice.” Since one is all, it is called “perfect voice.” As the Flower Garland Sūtra says, “In a single utterance he gives voice to every mode of speech of all beings, without remainder. Wishing to understand this pure, hidden voice in full, a bodhisattva first arouses the aspiration to awakening.”

What each sound pervades
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

Further, this voice of the Buddha is inconceivable. Each sound of speech is all sounds, and it pervades every dharma equally. I will give six pairs to show what this equal pervasion consists in. ↓

1. Beings and dharmas
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

First, it extends as far as all beings and all dharmas.

2. Space and time
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

Second, as far as all lands in the ten directions and all the eons of the past, present, and future.

3. Buddhas’ bodies
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

Third, as far as all tathāgatas in response bodies and all buddhas in transformation bodies.

4. Dharma realms and space
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

Fourth, as far as all dharma realms and the realm of space.

5. Mutual inclusion and arising
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

Fifth, as far as the realm of unobstructed mutual interpenetration and the realm of immeasurable arising.

6. Practice and nirvāṇa
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

Sixth, as far as the realm of all practices and the realm of peaceful nirvāṇa.

How pervasion preserves distinctions
BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

The Flower Garland Sūtra explains this in its discussion of the three kinds of nonobstruction. Each individual sound reaches as far as these six pairs, yet its tones and inflections are never confused. If there were anywhere in these six pairs that the voice did not reach, the voice would fall short of perfection.

BDK p. 6 ↗so that once he had preached with his perfect voice,

If in reaching everywhere it lost its particular melody, its perfection would cease to be that of a voice. Yet it reaches everywhere with its melody intact, and its tones differ with its pervasion undisturbed. Only so does it constitute a perfect voice. The deliberating mind cannot fathom this, for it expresses the freedom of the dharmakāya. So much for this brief account of the one voice. Let us end the digression and return to the text.

2. After the Buddha’s passing
BDK p. 6 ↗But after the passing away of the Tathāgata,

The second part describes the varying faculties and ways of practice after the Buddha’s passing. It distinguishes four kinds of disposition. Those of the first two kinds gain understanding through sūtras. Those of the latter two gain it only with the help of treatises. ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓

Through sūtras
1. Hearing much
BDK p. 6 ↗there were some who were able by their own power to listen extensively to others and to…

In the first case, “those who, by their own powers, can hear much and gain understanding” understand the Buddha’s intent by hearing the sūtras at length, without needing treatises. That is the meaning of “by their own powers.”

2. Hearing little
BDK p. 6 ↗there were some who by their own power could listen to very little and yet understand much;

In the second case, “those who likewise by their own powers hear little yet understand much” can deeply understand the sūtras’ intent without necessarily hearing their wording at length. They too can dispense with treatises, hence “by their own powers.”

Through treatises
3. Lengthy exposition
BDK p. 6 ↗there were some who, without an mental power of their own,

In the third case, “lacking the power of their own minds” describes people who cannot understand by relying on the Buddha’s discourses alone. This is what it means to lack that power. They understand what the Buddha means in the sūtras only with the aid of treatises such as the Great Perfection of Wisdom Treatise and the Yogācārabhūmi. Hence “those who gain understanding through extensive treatises.” †

extensive treatises · 廣論 guǎng lùn · BDK p. 6 extensive discourses of others
4. Concise exposition
BDK p. 6 ↗and naturally there were some who looked upon the wordiness of extensive discourses as…

In the fourth case, “those who find the many words of extensive treatises burdensome” have sharp faculties but little patience for prolixity. Only a treatise rich in meaning and sparing in words gives them a deep understanding of what the Buddha means in the sūtras. Hence “those who delight in grasping the whole and can understand when a few words encompass many meanings.”

BDK p. 6 ↗and who sought after what was comprehensive, terse, and yet contained much meaning,

Of these four, the first three are outside the scope of the present work. It was written for the fourth kind of person.

3. Conclusion
BDK p. 6 ↗Thus, this discourse is designed to embrace, in a general way, the limitless meaning of…

“In this way” begins the third part, which concludes the answer. “In this way” takes in all four kinds of people just discussed. “This treatise” and what follows singles out the fourth kind and concludes by making clear why the treatise must be written. The present treatise runs to only one scroll, yet takes in the intent of all the sūtras. Hence “because it encompasses the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma.” Those of the fourth kind, who delight in grasping the whole, need this treatise to awaken to the path. Hence “this treatise should be expounded.”

BDK p. 7

The mind of sentient beings

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 7 The principle is “the Mind of the sentient being.”⁕ This Mind includes in itself all states of being of the phenomenal world and the transcendental world. On the basis of this Mind, the meanings of the Mahayana may be unfolded. Why? Because the absolute aspect of this Mind represents the essence (svabhāva) of the Mahayana; and the phenomenal aspect of this Mind indicates the essence, attributes (lakṣana) and influences (kriyā) of the Mahayana itself.

Wŏnhyo · CommentaryT1844 ↗

2. Establishing the meaning

2. The two headings

2. Establishing the meaning › 2. The two headings

1. The dharma
1. The general statement
BDK p. 7 ↗The principle is “the Mind of the sentient being.”

In the first, the words “The dharma spoken of is the mind of sentient beings” mean the following. † What constitutes something in its own right is called its dharma. In the Great Vehicle, dharmas have no separate essence of their own. The One Mind alone constitutes their very essence. Hence the statement that the dharma is the mind of sentient beings.

mind of sentient beings · 眾生心 zhòng shēng xīn · BDK p. 7 the Mind of the sentient being
BDK p. 7 ↗This Mind includes in itself all states of being of the phenomenal world and the…

“This mind encompasses everything” distinguishes the dharma of the Great Vehicle from that of the Lesser Vehicle. For this mind encompasses all dharmas without exception, and the very essence of all dharmas is the One Mind alone. In the Lesser Vehicle, each dharma has its own essence. This is why the One Mind is spoken of as the dharma of the Great Vehicle.

2. The two gateways
BDK p. 7 ↗Why?

Beginning with “Why?” the text sets out the dharma separately under its gateways. This one passage serves two purposes. Looking back, it explains the general statement. Looking ahead, it sets out the individual gateways. The dharma of mind is one, yet the meaning of the Great Vehicle is vast. On what grounds can the meaning of the Great Vehicle be revealed on the basis of this mind alone? This is the point of asking “Why?” The explanation that follows means that although the dharma of mind is one, it has two gateways. In the gateway of suchness we find the essence of the Great Vehicle. ↓ In the gateway of arising and ceasing we find its essence, characteristics, and activity. † ↓ The meaning of the Great Vehicle extends no further than these three. Thus the One Mind reveals the meaning of the Great Vehicle.

“This mind as suchness” names the gateway of suchness as a whole † and introduces the passage below beginning “[It] is precisely the one dharmadhātu….” † † The next word, “characteristic,” means the characteristic of suchness. † It introduces the passage beginning “Furthermore, when suchness is distinguished in dependence on verbal expression, it has two [meanings]….”

1. The dharma
1. The general statement
BDK p. 7 ↗The principle is “the Mind of the sentient being.”

In the first of these two,

BDK p. 7 ↗The principle is “the Mind of the sentient being.”

the statement “The dharma is the mind of sentient beings” calls what constitutes something in its own right its dharma. † In the Great Vehicle, dharmas have no essence of their own. All take the One Mind as their very essence. Hence the statement that the dharma is the mind of sentient beings.

mind of sentient beings · 眾生心 zhòng shēng xīn · BDK p. 7 the Mind of the sentient being
BDK p. 7 ↗This Mind includes in itself all states of being of the phenomenal world and the…

“This mind encompasses all dharmas” distinguishes the dharma of the Great Vehicle from that of the Lesser Vehicle, for this mind encompasses all minds without exception.

BDK p. 7 ↗This Mind includes in itself all states of being of the phenomenal world and the…

“This mind encompasses all dharmas” shows that the very essence of the Great Vehicle’s dharma is the One Mind alone. In the Lesser Vehicle, each dharma has its own essence and can therefore count as a dharma in its own right. Hence the One Mind is spoken of as the dharma of the Great Vehicle. This is why the meaning of the Great Vehicle is revealed on the basis of this dharma of mind.

2. The two gateways
BDK p. 7 ↗Why?

Beginning with “Why?” the dharma is set out separately under its gateways. Looking back, the passage explains the general statement. Looking ahead, it sets out the individual gateways. The dharma of mind is one, while the Great Vehicle has many meanings. On what grounds, then, can the meaning of the Great Vehicle be revealed on the basis of this mind alone?

BDK p. 7 ↗Why?

The text beginning “Why?” gives the explanation. It means that although the dharma of mind is one, it has two gateways. BDK pp. 8–9

The three kinds of greatness and the vehicle

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 8 Of the significance [of the adjective mahā (great) in the compound, mahāyāna], there are three aspects: 1) the “greatness” of the essence, for all phenomena (dharmas) are identical with suchness and are neither increasing nor decreasing; 2) the “greatness” of the attributes, for the tathāgatagarbha is endowed with numberless excellent qualities; 3) the “greatness” of the influences, for the influences [of suchness] give rise to the good causes and effects in this and in the other world alike.

p. 9 [The significance of the term yāna (vehicle) in the compound, mahāyāna. The term yāna is introduced] because all Enlightened Ones (Buddhas) have ridden [on this vehicle], and all Enlightened Ones-to-be (bodhisattvas), being led by this principle, will reach the stage of Tathāgata.

2. The meaning of the name
BDK p. 8 ↗Of the significance [of the adjective mahā (great) in the compound, mahāyāna], there are…

What follows sets out the second heading, the meaning [of the name]. It too has two parts. The first clarifies “great.” The next explains “vehicle.” ↓ ↓ These likewise introduce passages in the later exposition. We shall match the passages to these statements when we reach them.

1. “Great”
BDK p. 8 ↗1) the “greatness” of the essence,

Of the meanings of “great,” greatness in essence belongs to the gateway of suchness. The other two, greatness in characteristics and in activity, belong to the gateway of arising and ceasing. The gateway of arising and ceasing also has its own essence. Here essence is taken together with characteristics, so it receives no separate mention.

BDK p. 8 ↗for the tathāgatagarbha is endowed with numberless excellent qualities;

“The tathāgatagarbha fully possesses immeasurable intrinsic virtues” refers, in one twofold classification of the garbha, to the nonempty tathāgatagarbha, and in another twofold classification, to the tathāgatagarbha in its capacity to encompass. Intrinsic virtues and greatness in activity will be treated in detail in the later exposition.

2. “Vehicle”
BDK p. 9 ↗[The significance of the term yāna (vehicle) in the compound, mahāyāna. The term yāna is…

Two statements bring out the meaning of “vehicle.” ↓ ↓

1. From fruit back to cause
BDK p. 9 ↗[The significance of the term yāna (vehicle) in the compound, mahāyāna. The term yāna is…

“Because all buddhas formerly rode it” explains “vehicle” by looking back from the fruit to its cause.

2. From cause forward to fruit
BDK p. 9 ↗and all Enlightened Ones-to-be (bodhisattvas), being led by this principle,

“Because all bodhisattvas ride this dharma and reach the stage of a tathāgata” explains “vehicle” by looking forward from the cause to its fruit.

2. Explanation following the text › The section establishing the meaning

2. The meaning of the name
BDK p. 8 ↗Of the significance [of the adjective mahā (great) in the compound, mahāyāna], there are…

Beginning with “As for the meaning…,” the text sets out its second heading, the meaning of the name. This too has two parts. The first explains “great” and the second “vehicle.” These two introduce two passages in the later exposition. We shall identify the corresponding passages when we reach them.

BDK p. 11

The divisions of the interpretation

BDK translationYoshito S. Hakeda

p. 11 The part on outline has been given; next the part on interpretation [of the principle of the Mahayana] will be given. It consists of three chapters: 1) Revelation of the True Meaning; 2) Correction of Evil Attachments; 3) Analysis of the Types of Aspiration for Enlightenment.

Interpretation

BDK 11 ↗The part on interpretation

The section on interpretation also falls into two parts.ᵀ

section on interpretation · 解釋分 jiě shì fēn · BDK p. 11 part on interpretation

  1. A transition closes the preceding section and opens the next.

2.2. The three divisions named
BDK 11 ↗Revelation of the True Meaning

In naming the divisions, “revealing the correct meaning” refers to the direct explanation of what was established in the Outline.ᵀ

revealing the correct meaning · 顯示正義 xiǎn shì zhèng yì · BDK p. 11 Revelation of the True Meaning

“Counteracting mistaken attachments” and “the characteristics of setting out toward the path” explain how to leave error behind and turn toward what is correct.ᵀ

The separate explanations thus occupy three chapters.

The “Revelation of the True Meaning” has two main divisions.

  2. Beginning “Furthermore, from the gateway of arising and ceasing,” a brief account of how to inquire into and enter reality.ᵀ
